tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

1	# Carma shared context
2	
3	Every carma-* skill reads this file first. It is the compact form of the "Carma PoC: Core Design Principles" document plus the constraints agreed with the client. When a skill's output has to choose between options, these principles are the tie-breakers, so cite them by number (P1, P6, ...) in specs.
4	
5	## 1. What we are building
6	
7	A proof of concept for Carma, a media intelligence company that aggregates online content (news, social, broadcast, print) and delivers it to PR and communications clients. The PoC is an **internal tool**. Its job is to **prepare data and make it searchable**. Client-facing presentation, export and sharing come later in the pipeline and are out of scope (see "Deferred" below).
8	
9	## 2. Agreed constraints
10	
11	| Area | Decision |
12	| --- | --- |
13	| Backing store | PostgreSQL. Carma's internal limitations rule out an event-driven platform such as Kafka for now. Queues, retries and processing state therefore live in the database or in-process. |
14	| Volume | About 800 articles per second, roughly 69 million a day. Maximise throughput; capacity is measured against this load. |
15	| Latency target | A brand mention reaches a user within 15 minutes of the article's `published_at` time, for every source and language. Insights are delivered daily or weekly and are not held to this target. |
16	| Priority on conflict | Completeness beats speed. A late item is better than a missed one. Items that miss the target are flagged, not dropped. |
17	| Input data | Articles only: `id`, `headline`, `body`, `source`, `published_at` (UTC timestamp), `language`. Other source types are out of scope. |
18	| Content fidelity | The emphasis is on text content. Storing exact, replicable HTML is not a goal. Headline and body are kept as text and are the system of record. Any markup is reduced to text during validation, and the reduction is recorded as a transformation. Raw markup is not retained by default. A hash of the received payload is kept for integrity and dedupe. |
19	| Deployment | Everything runs under Docker Compose on the target machine: database, web app, workers, observability. `docker compose up` on that machine must set everything up automatically (migrations, roles, extensions, secrets, dashboards). Keys and secrets are handled as configuration, never committed. Compose is single-host, so capacity fit against the 800/s target is checked rather than assumed. |
20	| Languages | English, Arabic and Chinese are in scope for the exercise. Nothing may hard-code those three: any language must work through the same data model. |
21	| Confidence scale | One 0 to 100% scale for every derived field. Scorers usually report on 0 to 1 or another range, so a min/max range is supplied per scoring source and values are normalised. |
22	| Fields needing confidence | Sentiment, relevance, topic, summary, entity match. |
23	| Calibration | Out of scope. Transparency (P7) lets a human or agent decide whether a value is acceptable. |
24	| Evidence base | Carma's public website only. Carma is assumed to agree with the principles. |
25	
26	Illustrative sizing, to be replaced by measurement: 800/s is 48,000 a minute and 2.88 million an hour. The 15-minute window therefore holds about 720,000 articles in flight. At 1 ms of CPU per article the pipeline needs 0.8 cores, at 10 ms it needs 8, at 100 ms it needs 80, so per-article cost is the first thing to question. At 1 to 5 KB of text per article, raw storage is roughly 69 to 345 GB a day before indexes and WAL, so retention and partitioning are first-order design concerns.
27	
28	The sample article in the brief is about 500 characters, shorter than a typical real article. Treat it as a schema example, not a size benchmark.
29	
30	## 3. Principles
31	
32	Use these as design tests: "which principle does this choice serve, and which does it cost?"
33	
34	| # | Principle | In one line | Ask yourself |
35	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
36	| P1 | Fast | Published to visible with minimal delay; clock starts at `published_at` | Is capture lag measured separately from processing time? Can fresh items be searchable before enrichment finishes? |
37	| P2 | Reliable | Predictable; failures are never silent | What happens on crash, retry, duplicate delivery, backlog? Is processing state recorded so work can resume? |
38	| P3 | Complete, honest about gaps | Broad coverage; what is not covered is visible | Can a user tell "no results" from "not covered" from "not yet processed"? Does any path drop an item? |
39	| P4 | Signal over volume | Noise is a defect | Are dedupe/filter/rank decisions recorded so removed content is recoverable? |
40	| P5 | Consistent across markets and languages | Same data model and field definitions everywhere | Does anything assume Latin script, spaces between words, or left-to-right text? |
41	| P6 | Every insight carries a confidence | 0 to 100% on every derived field, visible by default | Does every derived field have a confidence, or an explicit "no confidence available"? |
42	| P7 | Confidence is inspectable | Origin and method stated plainly, even if unimpressive | Do we store origin, method, inputs, raw value, min/max range and normalised value? |
43	| P8 | Everything traces to its source | Any item can be followed back to the original content | Does each derived item reference its source items and the processing applied? |
44	| P9 | Human judgment is part of the system | Automation and people have defined, visible roles | Where can an analyst review, correct or override? Is output marked automated, human-reviewed or human-authored? |
45	| P10 | Data leads to meaning | Explain what happened and why it matters | Does the data model carry the context needed for explanation (topic, entities, sentiment, relationships)? |
46	| P11 | Fit the audience | Content suits the person and situation | Can urgency, audience and market be filtered and derived later? |
47	
48	Priority order when principles conflict: P3 (completeness) outranks P1 (speed) per the client. P2 and P6 to P8 are not traded away for throughput without an explicit decision from the user.
49	
50	### Confidence model (P6, P7)
51	
52	Every derived value stores: the normalised confidence (0 to 100), the raw score, the min/max range of the scoring source, the origin type, the method and its version, and when it was produced. Origins we expect: model self-report (an LLM stating "60% confident"), rule-based, statistical or classifier score, human review, combined. A 60 from a model's self-report and a 60 from a classifier mean different things, so the origin always travels with the number. Never present a self-reported LLM figure as a statistical probability.
53	
54	### Deferred (do not design for now)
55	
56	Shareable-by-default outputs: executive briefings, branded newsletters, ready-made reports, exports. Keep data models from making these harder later (P11), nothing more.
57	
58	## 4. Known unknowns
59	
60	These are unverified. If a design depends on one, say so in the spec and ask.
61	
62	- `published_at` is source-supplied and assumed accurate. Missing, future-dated or wrong values would corrupt the 15-minute clock.
63	- Whether `id` is globally unique or only unique per source.
64	- Whether bodies arrive as plain text or HTML (the sample is plain text). Original markup is assumed not needed for now; revisit if a requirement changes.
65	- Target machine specs (CPU, memory, disk, OS), whether it has internet access to pull images, and whether images are built in CI or on the target.
66	- Real average article size, source mix and language mix.
67	- PostgreSQL version, hosting model and which extensions are permitted in Carma's environment.
68	- Which brand or query sets drive "brand mention" detection, and how many standing queries exist.
69	
70	## 5. Spec conventions (when run inside a codebase)
71	
72	Skills write their output as numbered markdown files so decisions and reasoning survive the conversation and later skills can read them.
73	
74	| Skill | Output directory |
75	| --- | --- |
76	| carma-architect (raw design docs) | `.specs/architect/` |
77	| carma-architect (approved decisions) | `.specs/architect/adrs/` |
78	| carma-searchability | `.specs/search/` |
79	| carma-telemetry | `.specs/telemetry/` |
80	| carma-data-sanity | `.specs/data/sanitization/` |
81	| carma-dba | `.specs/data/dba/` |
82	| carma-backend-testing | `.specs/testing/backend/` |
83	| carma-devops | `.specs/devops/` |
84	| carma-ux | `.specs/ux/` |
85	| carma-review (runs outside the main flow) | `.specs/review/` |
86	| carma-benchmark (runs outside the main flow) | `.benchmarks/<feature>/` (executable Node.js files, not numbered specs) |
87	| carma-plan | `.specs/plan/` |
88	
89	**"In a codebase" means** the working directory is a project: it has a `.git` directory or a recognisable manifest (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, `pom.xml`, `Cargo.toml`, `*.csproj`, etc.) or a source tree. If it is not, do not create files. Deliver the output in the conversation and offer to save it once a project is available.
90	
91	**Numbering.** Each directory has its own sequence of four-digit numbers: `0001-short-slug.md`, `0002-...`. Get the next number with `scripts/next_spec_number.py <directory>`, which also creates the directory if it is missing. Never reuse or renumber a file. Edit a spec in place while its status is `draft`; once it is `approved`, a change is a new file whose front matter says `supersedes`.
92	
93	**Front matter** on every spec:
94	
95	```yaml
96	---
97	spec: carma-dba            # skill that produced it
98	number: 0003
99	title: Partitioned storage for article ingestion
100	status: draft              # draft | in-review | approved | superseded
101	date: 2026-10-24
102	feature: article-ingestion # short name shared across the specs for one feature
103	inputs: [.specs/architect/0002-article-ingestion.md]
104	principles: [P1, P2, P3]
105	supersedes: null
106	---
107	```
108	
109	**Finding inputs.** Upstream specs for the same `feature` are the input. List the relevant directory, read the highest-numbered non-superseded spec for that feature (plus any ADRs that reference it), and record the paths under `inputs`. If an expected input is missing, say so and either run the upstream skill's analysis inline or ask the user, rather than guessing.
110	
111	## 6. When to ask the user
112	
113	Ask when a requirement is ambiguous, when two priorities conflict and the principles above do not settle it, or when a choice is expensive to reverse. Do not ask what the constraints above already answer, and do not ask what you can find by reading the codebase.
114	
115	Ask with the AskUserQuestion tool when it is available (one to four questions, two to four options each, recommended option first and marked). Each option needs its trade-off in one line: what it gains, what it costs, which principles it touches. If the tool is not available, ask in plain text with the same structure. If nobody is available to answer (an unattended or scheduled run), pick the option that best matches the principles, mark it `UNCONFIRMED` in the spec, and list it under open questions so it is not mistaken for a decision.
116	
117	Group questions: one round of well-formed questions beats a stream of single ones.
118

When a skill's output has to choose between options, these principles are the tie-breakers, so cite them by number (P1, P6, ...) in specs.

## 1. What we are building

A proof of concept for Carma, a media intelligence company that aggregates online content (news, social, broadcast, print) and delivers it to PR and communications clients. The PoC is an **internal tool**. Its job is to **prepare data and make it searchable**. Client-facing presentation, export and sharing come later in the pipeline and are out of scope (see "Deferred" below).

## 2. Agreed constraints

| Area | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| Backing store | PostgreSQL. Carma's internal limitations rule out an event-driven platform such as Kafka for now. Queues, retries and processing state therefore live in the database or in-process. |
| Volume | About 800 articles per second, roughly 69 million a day. Maximise throughput; capacity is measured against this load. |
| Latency target | A brand mention reaches a user within 15 minutes of the article's `published_at` time, for every source and language. Insights are delivered daily or weekly and are not held to this target. |
| Priority on conflict | Completeness beats speed. A late item is better than a missed one. Items that miss the target are flagged, not dropped. |
| Input data | Articles only: `id`, `headline`, `body`, `source`, `published_at` (UTC timestamp), `language`. Other source types are out of scope. |
| Content fidelity | The emphasis is on text content. Storing exact, replicable HTML is not a goal. Headline and body are kept as text and are the system of record. Any markup is reduced to text during validation, and the reduction is recorded as a transformation. Raw markup is not retained by default. A hash of the received payload is kept for integrity and dedupe. |
| Deployment | Everything runs under Docker Compose on the target machine: database, web app, workers, observability. `docker compose up` on that machine must set everything up automatically (migrations, roles, extensions, secrets, dashboards). Keys and secrets are handled as configuration, never committed. Compose is single-host, so capacity fit against the 800/s target is checked rather than assumed. |
| Languages | English, Arabic and Chinese are in scope for the exercise. Nothing may hard-code those three: any language must work through the same data model. |
| Confidence scale | One 0 to 100% scale for every derived field. Scorers usually report on 0 to 1 or another range, so a min/max range is supplied per scoring source and values are normalised. |
| Fields needing confidence | Sentiment, relevance, topic, summary, entity match. |
| Calibration | Out of scope. Transparency (P7) lets a human or agent decide whether a value is acceptable. |
| Evidence base | Carma's public website only. Carma is assumed to agree with the principles. |

Illustrative sizing, to be replaced by measurement: 800/s is 48,000 a minute and 2.88 million an hour. The 15-minute window therefore holds about 720,000 articles in flight. At 1 ms of CPU per article the pipeline needs 0.8 cores, at 10 ms it needs 8, at 100 ms it needs 80, so per-article cost is the first thing to question. At 1 to 5 KB of text per article, raw storage is roughly 69 to 345 GB a day before indexes and WAL, so retention and partitioning are first-order design concerns.

The sample article in the brief is about 500 characters, shorter than a typical real article. Treat it as a schema example, not a size benchmark.

## 3. Principles

Use these as design tests: "which principle does this choice serve, and which does it cost?"

| # | Principle | In one line | Ask yourself |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | Fast | Published to visible with minimal delay; clock starts at `published_at` | Is capture lag measured separately from processing time? Can fresh items be searchable before enrichment finishes? |
| P2 | Reliable | Predictable; failures are never silent | What happens on crash, retry, duplicate delivery, backlog? Is processing state recorded so work can resume? |
| P3 | Complete, honest about gaps | Broad coverage; what is not covered is visible | Can a user tell "no results" from "not covered" from "not yet processed"? Does any path drop an item? |
| P4 | Signal over volume | Noise is a defect | Are dedupe/filter/rank decisions recorded so removed content is recoverable? |
| P5 | Consistent across markets and languages | Same data model and field definitions everywhere | Does anything assume Latin script, spaces between words, or left-to-right text? |
| P6 | Every insight carries a confidence | 0 to 100% on every derived field, visible by default | Does every derived field have a confidence, or an explicit "no confidence available"? |
| P7 | Confidence is inspectable | Origin and method stated plainly, even if unimpressive | Do we store origin, method, inputs, raw value, min/max range and normalised value? |
| P8 | Everything traces to its source | Any item can be followed back to the original content | Does each derived item reference its source items and the processing applied? |
| P9 | Human judgment is part of the system | Automation and people have defined, visible roles | Where can an analyst review, correct or override? Is output marked automated, human-reviewed or human-authored? |
| P10 | Data leads to meaning | Explain what happened and why it matters | Does the data model carry the context needed for explanation (topic, entities, sentiment, relationships)? |
| P11 | Fit the audience | Content suits the person and situation | Can urgency, audience and market be filtered and derived later? |

Priority order when principles conflict: P3 (completeness) outranks P1 (speed) per the client. P2 and P6 to P8 are not traded away for throughput without an explicit decision from the user.

### Confidence model (P6, P7)

Every derived value stores: the normalised confidence (0 to 100), the raw score, the min/max range of the scoring source, the origin type, the method and its version, and when it was produced. Origins we expect: model self-report (an LLM stating "60% confident"), rule-based, statistical or classifier score, human review, combined. A 60 from a model's self-report and a 60 from a classifier mean different things, so the origin always travels with the number. Never present a self-reported LLM figure as a statistical probability.

### Deferred (do not design for now)

Shareable-by-default outputs: executive briefings, branded newsletters, ready-made reports, exports. Keep data models from making these harder later (P11), nothing more.

## 4. Known unknowns

These are unverified. If a design depends on one, say so in the spec and ask.

- `published_at` is source-supplied and assumed accurate. Missing, future-dated or wrong values would corrupt the 15-minute clock.
- Whether `id` is globally unique or only unique per source.
- Whether bodies arrive as plain text or HTML (the sample is plain text). Original markup is assumed not needed for now; revisit if a requirement changes.
- Target machine specs (CPU, memory, disk, OS), whether it has internet access to pull images, and whether images are built in CI or on the target.
- Real average article size, source mix and language mix.
- PostgreSQL version, hosting model and which extensions are permitted in Carma's environment.
- Which brand or query sets drive "brand mention" detection, and how many standing queries exist.

## 5. Spec conventions (when run inside a codebase)

Skills write their output as numbered markdown files so decisions and reasoning survive the conversation and later skills can read them.

| Skill | Output directory |
| --- | --- |
| carma-architect (raw design docs) | `.specs/architect/` |
| carma-architect (approved decisions) | `.specs/architect/adrs/` |
| carma-searchability | `.specs/search/` |
| carma-telemetry | `.specs/telemetry/` |
| carma-data-sanity | `.specs/data/sanitization/` |
| carma-dba | `.specs/data/dba/` |
| carma-backend-testing | `.specs/testing/backend/` |
| carma-devops | `.specs/devops/` |
| carma-ux | `.specs/ux/` |
| carma-review (runs outside the main flow) | `.specs/review/` |
| carma-benchmark (runs outside the main flow) | `.benchmarks/<feature>/` (executable Node.js files, not numbered specs) |
| carma-plan | `.specs/plan/` |

**"In a codebase" means** the working directory is a project: it has a `.git` directory or a recognisable manifest (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, `pom.xml`, `Cargo.toml`, `*.csproj`, etc.) or a source tree. If it is not, do not create files. Deliver the output in the conversation and offer to save it once a project is available.

**Numbering.** Each directory has its own sequence of four-digit numbers: `0001-short-slug.md`, `0002-...`. Get the next number with `scripts/next_spec_number.py <directory>`, which also creates the directory if it is missing. Never reuse or renumber a file. Edit a spec in place while its status is `draft`; once it is `approved`, a change is a new file whose front matter says `supersedes`.

**Front matter** on every spec:

```yaml
---
spec: carma-dba            # skill that produced it
number: 0003
title: Partitioned storage for article ingestion
status: draft              # draft | in-review | approved | superseded
date: 2026-10-24
feature: article-ingestion # short name shared across the specs for one feature
inputs: [.specs/architect/0002-article-ingestion.md]
principles: [P1, P2, P3]
supersedes: null
---
```

**Finding inputs.** Upstream specs for the same `feature` are the input. List the relevant directory, read the highest-numbered non-superseded spec for that feature (plus any ADRs that reference it), and record the paths under `inputs`. If an expected input is missing, say so and either run the upstream skill's analysis inline or ask the user, rather than guessing.

## 6. When to ask the user

Ask when a requirement is ambiguous, when two priorities conflict and the principles above do not settle it, or when a choice is expensive to reverse. Do not ask what the constraints above already answer, and do not ask what you can find by reading the codebase.

Ask with the AskUserQuestion tool when it is available (one to four questions, two to four options each, recommended option first and marked). Each option needs its trade-off in one line: what it gains, what it costs, which principles it touches. If the tool is not available, ask in plain text with the same structure. If nobody is available to answer (an unattended or scheduled run), pick the option that best matches the principles, mark it `UNCONFIRMED` in the spec, and list it under open questions so it is not mistaken for a decision.

Group questions: one round of well-formed questions beats a stream of single ones.

content.content:
1	# Carma shared context
2	
3	Every carma-* skill reads this file first. It is the compact form of the "Carma PoC: Core Design Principles" document plus the constraints agreed with the client. When a skill's output has to choose between options, these principles are the tie-breakers, so cite them by number (P1, P6, ...) in specs.
4	
5	## 1. What we are building
6	
7	A proof of concept for Carma, a media intelligence company that aggregates online content (news, social, broadcast, print) and delivers it to PR and communications clients. The PoC is an **internal tool**. Its job is to **prepare data and make it searchable**. Client-facing presentation, export and sharing come later in the pipeline and are out of scope (see "Deferred" below).
8	
9	## 2. Agreed constraints
10	
11	| Area | Decision |
12	| --- | --- |
13	| Backing store | PostgreSQL. Carma's internal limitations rule out an event-driven platform such as Kafka for now. Queues, retries and processing state therefore live in the database or in-process. |
14	| Volume | About 800 articles per second, roughly 69 million a day. Maximise throughput; capacity is measured against this load. |
15	| Latency target | A brand mention reaches a user within 15 minutes of the article's `published_at` time, for every source and language. Insights are delivered daily or weekly and are not held to this target. |
16	| Priority on conflict | Completeness beats speed. A late item is better than a missed one. Items that miss the target are flagged, not dropped. |
17	| Input data | Articles only: `id`, `headline`, `body`, `source`, `published_at` (UTC timestamp), `language`. Other source types are out of scope. |
18	| Content fidelity | The emphasis is on text content. Storing exact, replicable HTML is not a goal. Headline and body are kept as text and are the system of record. Any markup is reduced to text during validation, and the reduction is recorded as a transformation. Raw markup is not retained by default. A hash of the received payload is kept for integrity and dedupe. |
19	| Deployment | Everything runs under Docker Compose on the target machine: database, web app, workers, observability. `docker compose up` on that machine must set everything up automatically (migrations, roles, extensions, secrets, dashboards). Keys and secrets are handled as configuration, never committed. Compose is single-host, so capacity fit against the 800/s target is checked rather than assumed. |
20	| Languages | English, Arabic and Chinese are in scope for the exercise. Nothing may hard-code those three: any language must work through the same data model. |
21	| Confidence scale | One 0 to 100% scale for every derived field. Scorers usually report on 0 to 1 or another range, so a min/max range is supplied per scoring source and values are normalised. |
22	| Fields needing confidence | Sentiment, relevance, topic, summary, entity match. |
23	| Calibration | Out of scope. Transparency (P7) lets a human or agent decide whether a value is acceptable. |
24	| Evidence base | Carma's public website only. Carma is assumed to agree with the principles. |
25	
26	Illustrative sizing, to be replaced by measurement: 800/s is 48,000 a minute and 2.88 million an hour. The 15-minute window therefore holds about 720,000 articles in flight. At 1 ms of CPU per article the pipeline needs 0.8 cores, at 10 ms it needs 8, at 100 ms it needs 80, so per-article cost is the first thing to question. At 1 to 5 KB of text per article, raw storage is roughly 69 to 345 GB a day before indexes and WAL, so retention and partitioning are first-order design concerns.
27	
28	The sample article in the brief is about 500 characters, shorter than a typical real article. Treat it as a schema example, not a size benchmark.
29	
30	## 3. Principles
31	
32	Use these as design tests: "which principle does this choice serve, and which does it cost?"
33	
34	| # | Principle | In one line | Ask yourself |
35	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
36	| P1 | Fast | Published to visible with minimal delay; clock starts at `published_at` | Is capture lag measured separately from processing time? Can fresh items be searchable before enrichment finishes? |
37	| P2 | Reliable | Predictable; failures are never silent | What happens on crash, retry, duplicate delivery, backlog? Is processing state recorded so work can resume? |
38	| P3 | Complete, honest about gaps | Broad coverage; what is not covered is visible | Can a user tell "no results" from "not covered" from "not yet processed"? Does any path drop an item? |
39	| P4 | Signal over volume | Noise is a defect | Are dedupe/filter/rank decisions recorded so removed content is recoverable? |
40	| P5 | Consistent across markets and languages | Same data model and field definitions everywhere | Does anything assume Latin script, spaces between words, or left-to-right text? |
41	| P6 | Every insight carries a confidence | 0 to 100% on every derived field, visible by default | Does every derived field have a confidence, or an explicit "no confidence available"? |
42	| P7 | Confidence is inspectable | Origin and method stated plainly, even if unimpressive | Do we store origin, method, inputs, raw value, min/max range and normalised value? |
43	| P8 | Everything traces to its source | Any item can be followed back to the original content | Does each derived item reference its source items and the processing applied? |
44	| P9 | Human judgment is part of the system | Automation and people have defined, visible roles | Where can an analyst review, correct or override? Is output marked automated, human-reviewed or human-authored? |
45	| P10 | Data leads to meaning | Explain what happened and why it matters | Does the data model carry the context needed for explanation (topic, entities, sentiment, relationships)? |
46	| P11 | Fit the audience | Content suits the person and situation | Can urgency, audience and market be filtered and derived later? |
47	
48	Priority order when principles conflict: P3 (completeness) outranks P1 (speed) per the client. P2 and P6 to P8 are not traded away for throughput without an explicit decision from the user.
49	
50	### Confidence model (P6, P7)
51	
52	Every derived value stores: the normalised confidence (0 to 100), the raw score, the min/max range of the scoring source, the origin type, the method and its version, and when it was produced. Origins we expect: model self-report (an LLM stating "60% confident"), rule-based, statistical or classifier score, human review, combined. A 60 from a model's self-report and a 60 from a classifier mean different things, so the origin always travels with the number. Never present a self-reported LLM figure as a statistical probability.
53	
54	### Deferred (do not design for now)
55	
56	Shareable-by-default outputs: executive briefings, branded newsletters, ready-made reports, exports. Keep data models from making these harder later (P11), nothing more.
57	
58	## 4. Known unknowns
59	
60	These are unverified. If a design depends on one, say so in the spec and ask.
61	
62	- `published_at` is source-supplied and assumed accurate. Missing, future-dated or wrong values would corrupt the 15-minute clock.
63	- Whether `id` is globally unique or only unique per source.
64	- Whether bodies arrive as plain text or HTML (the sample is plain text). Original markup is assumed not needed for now; revisit if a requirement changes.
65	- Target machine specs (CPU, memory, disk, OS), whether it has internet access to pull images, and whether images are built in CI or on the target.
66	- Real average article size, source mix and language mix.
67	- PostgreSQL version, hosting model and which extensions are permitted in Carma's environment.
68	- Which brand or query sets drive "brand mention" detection, and how many standing queries exist.
69	
70	## 5. Spec conventions (when run inside a codebase)
71	
72	Skills write their output as numbered markdown files so decisions and reasoning survive the conversation and later skills can read them.
73	
74	| Skill | Output directory |
75	| --- | --- |
76	| carma-architect (raw design docs) | `.specs/architect/` |
77	| carma-architect (approved decisions) | `.specs/architect/adrs/` |
78	| carma-searchability | `.specs/search/` |
79	| carma-telemetry | `.specs/telemetry/` |
80	| carma-data-sanity | `.specs/data/sanitization/` |
81	| carma-dba | `.specs/data/dba/` |
82	| carma-backend-testing | `.specs/testing/backend/` |
83	| carma-devops | `.specs/devops/` |
84	| carma-ux | `.specs/ux/` |
85	| carma-review (runs outside the main flow) | `.specs/review/` |
86	| carma-benchmark (runs outside the main flow) | `.benchmarks/<feature>/` (executable Node.js files, not numbered specs) |
87	| carma-plan | `.specs/plan/` |
88	
89	**"In a codebase" means** the working directory is a project: it has a `.git` directory or a recognisable manifest (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, `pom.xml`, `Cargo.toml`, `*.csproj`, etc.) or a source tree. If it is not, do not create files. Deliver the output in the conversation and offer to save it once a project is available.
90	
91	**Numbering.** Each directory has its own sequence of four-digit numbers: `0001-short-slug.md`, `0002-...`. Get the next number with `scripts/next_spec_number.py <directory>`, which also creates the directory if it is missing. Never reuse or renumber a file. Edit a spec in place while its status is `draft`; once it is `approved`, a change is a new file whose front matter says `supersedes`.
92	
93	**Front matter** on every spec:
94	
95	```yaml
96	---
97	spec: carma-dba            # skill that produced it
98	number: 0003
99	title: Partitioned storage for article ingestion
100	status: draft              # draft | in-review | approved | superseded
101	date: 2026-10-24
102	feature: article-ingestion # short name shared across the specs for one feature
103	inputs: [.specs/architect/0002-article-ingestion.md]
104	principles: [P1, P2, P3]
105	supersedes: null
106	---
107	```
108	
109	**Finding inputs.** Upstream specs for the same `feature` are the input. List the relevant directory, read the highest-numbered non-superseded spec for that feature (plus any ADRs that reference it), and record the paths under `inputs`. If an expected input is missing, say so and either run the upstream skill's analysis inline or ask the user, rather than guessing.
110	
111	## 6. When to ask the user
112	
113	Ask when a requirement is ambiguous, when two priorities conflict and the principles above do not settle it, or when a choice is expensive to reverse. Do not ask what the constraints above already answer, and do not ask what you can find by reading the codebase.
114	
115	Ask with the AskUserQuestion tool when it is available (one to four questions, two to four options each, recommended option first and marked). Each option needs its trade-off in one line: what it gains, what it costs, which principles it touches. If the tool is not available, ask in plain text with the same structure. If nobody is available to answer (an unattended or scheduled run), pick the option that best matches the principles, mark it `UNCONFIRMED` in the spec, and list it under open questions so it is not mistaken for a decision.
116	
117	Group questions: one round of well-formed questions beats a stream of single ones.
118

12	
13	# 0004 Plan for English-first display and default stemmed/substring search
14	
15	## 1. Summary
16	Build two changes on the shipped translation feature: (1) English-first headlines and text with the original underneath, and (2) default search that matches English word forms and partial words, with quotes for exact matches and summaries made searchable. Two phases, about 22 to 31 hours in total. Critical path: migration (four concurrent indexes) → compiler → list query → plan tests → UI. The database and query work (phase 1) must land before the UI (phase 2) can show matched sides and English excerpts.
17	
18	## 2. Inputs
19	All specs and ADRs in the front matter, present and read. Skipped by choice: carma-devops (nothing new to run; the migration-at-start-up concern is a task here) and carma-data-sanity (ILIKE escaping and escaped rendering are covered in test tasks). Mode: sequential. Specs were amended in place (still drafts) after the late decisions in ADR-0035; they were not re-run.
20	
21	## 3. Blockers and open questions
22	No blockers. Open items to track (all have a safe default):
23	| # | Item | Owner | Default if unanswered |
24	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
25	| Q1 | Summary language: assumed English | Human, check 20 real summaries in phase 1 | English |
26	| Q2 | Wording of the "no summary yet" coverage line | Human | Wording in UX 0004 section 5.5 |
27	| Q3 | "Machine translated" tag on every translated card | Human | Every card |
28	| Q4 | `pg_trgm` enabled in the target database | Human, T1.2 | Flag `trgm_index` decides at runtime |
29	| Q5 | Index size and write cost at 800/s | Human, after B1 | Extrapolation only, labelled |
30	| Q6 | Keep legacy beacon values one release | Human | Keep |
31	
32	## 4. Consistency report
33	| # | Finding | Class | Resolution |
34	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
35	| C1 | Architect 0004 sections 1 and 5.3 say "no migration expected"; ADR-0030/0034/0035 require migration 0007 | Note | Decisions recorded section of architect 0004 says so; T1.2 is the migration; edit the two sentences when the architect spec is approved |
36	| C2 | Search 0003 section 6 still says "`articles(search_vector_en)` GIN" and "no new trigram index"; ADR-0034 uses expression indexes and ADR-0035 adds a summary trigram index | Note | Section 3 and 14 were amended; fix section 6 wording in T1.5 |
37	| C3 | Architect 0004 FP-1/HP-2 describe an application stem function; stemming is now Postgres's English config | Note | Treat FP-1 as "stem collisions" only; HP-2 is void |
38	| C4 | ADR-0030 says "generated"; ADR-0034 supersedes that wording | Note | ADR-0034 governs |
39	| C5 | DBA 0001 says nothing updates `articles`; versions now update it (`0003_article_versions.sql`) | Note | The new partial index is maintained on update; covered by the version test |
40	| C6 | Telemetry reuses the `query` label key for index names and uses `kind` with different value sets on two metrics | Risk | Acceptable under the label allow-list; rename in a follow-up if confusing; T2.6 checks the label test |
41	| C7 | UX 0004 open question: `ArticleCard` sets `lang` of the AI summary from the article language, wrong if the summary is English | Risk | T2.2 checks and fixes `lang="en"` for summaries if Q1 is yes |
42	| C8 | Search on summaries only works after enrichment; unenriched articles miss summary matches | Risk | Coverage line (T2.4); P3 |
43	| C9 | The `articles` partial index predicate must be repeated textually by the query | Risk | Plan test P7 (T1.6) |
44	| C10 | Quoted-term matching on summaries has no dedicated index (rechecked on narrowed rows) | Risk | Experiment E9 in T1.6; add an index only if the plan test shows a problem |
45	| C11 | Late decision: foreign originals are not English-stemmed. Recall for English words inside foreign originals depends on the substring branch | Note | Golden cases G8, G14 document it |
46	| C12 | Unvalidated assumptions from the context file: real foreign share, article size, PostgreSQL extension permissions | Risk | First experiment in T1.6 replaces the guesses |
47	No principle conflict is unrecorded: P3 over P4 (broader default) is ADR-0033; precision path is ADR-0031.
48	
49	## 5. Dependency graph
50	| Task | Depends on |
51	| --- | --- |
52	| T1.1 Seed helper and fixtures | none |
53	| T1.2 Migration 0007 | T1.1 (for the test) |
54	| T1.3 Migration test | T1.2 |
55	| T1.4 Compiler and operator-matrix tests | none (parallel with T1.2) |
56	| T1.5 List query and match sides | T1.2, T1.4 |
57	| T1.6 Integration golden and plan tests | T1.3, T1.5 |
58	| T1.7 Benchmark B1 and review gate | T1.6 |
59	| T2.1 Headline-pair function | none (can start in phase 1) |
60	| T2.2 Search card | T1.5, T2.1 |
61	| T2.3 Article page | T2.1 |
62	| T2.4 Echo, notes, strings, coverage line | T1.4 |
63	| T2.5 Matched-side marker | T1.5 |
64	| T2.6 Beacon, metrics, alerts, dashboards | T1.5, T2.3 |
65	| T2.7 End-to-end keyboard and no-JS tests | T2.2, T2.3 |
66	| T2.8 Benchmark B2, review gate, spec close-out | T2.2 to T2.7 |
67	```
68	T1.1 → T1.2 → T1.3 ─┐
69	T1.4 ───────────────┼→ T1.5 → T1.6 → T1.7 → [phase 2]
70	T2.1 ─(parallel)────┘
71	```
72	Critical path: T1.1, T1.2, T1.5, T1.6, then T2.2/T2.5, T2.7, T2.8. Parallel: T1.4 and T2.1 can run beside the migration work (different files).
73	
74	## 6. Phases
75	
76	### Phase 1: Search data layer and query (about 12 to 16 hours)
77	Goal: unquoted Latin terms find English word forms and partial words across original, translation and summary, quoted terms stay exact, and plans use the new indexes.
78	Entry criteria: ADR-0030 to 0035 accepted (done); no blockers.
79	Rollback or safe-stop: drop the four indexes concurrently; the compiler change is behind the same commit, so revert it too. Search then returns to the previous behaviour; no data changed.
80	Human checkpoints: T1.6 plan inspection; T1.7 benchmark review.
81	
82	**T1.1 Add seeding helper and fixtures** (agent, 1 to 2 h)
83	- Why: plan tests and golden cases need 20,000+ articles with foreign rows, translations and summaries (testing 0004 sections 3.1, 7).
84	- Steps: extend `tests/harness/db.ts` with a seeded bulk loader; extend `tests/fixtures/articles.ts` and `tests/fixtures/translation.ts` with inflection pairs (startup/startups, enterprise/enterprises, news), `und` and `en-GB` labels, Arabic/French/Chinese rows, current and non-current summaries via `derived_values`; reuse the seeded generator in `.benchmarks/article-ingest/bench-lib.mjs`.
85	- Where: `tests/harness/db.ts`, `tests/fixtures/`.
86	- Output: a helper that seeds N rows with a fixed seed and runs `ANALYZE`.
87	- Acceptance: deterministic row counts across two runs; foreign share 30 percent.
88	- Depends on: none. Spec refs: testing 0004 sections 3.1, 7.
89	
90	**T1.2 Write migration 0007: four concurrent expression indexes** (agent, 2 to 3 h)
91	- Why: ADR-0030, 0034, 0035; DBA 0004 sections 4 and 4.1; FP-DB1 to FP-DB4.
92	- Steps: new `db/migrations/0007_english_search_indexes.sql` starting with `-- no-transaction`. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS` for: `articles_fts_en_idx` (`to_tsvector('english', search_text)` where `split_part(language, '-', 1) IN ('en','und')`), `article_translations_fts_en_idx` (same expression, `WHERE superseded_at IS NULL`), `derived_values_summary_fts_en_idx` (`to_tsvector('english', value)` where `field = 'summary' AND is_current`), `derived_values_summary_trgm_idx` (`gin_trgm_ops`, same predicate; skip with the `trgm_index` flag when `pg_trgm` is off). After building, drop any index with `indisvalid = false` first (re-run safe) and fail if one remains invalid. Run `pg_get_keywords()` on the new identifiers.
93	- Where: `db/migrations/`; the runner in `src/lib/db/migrate.ts` already supports `-- no-transaction`.
94	- Acceptance: migration applies on an empty and on a seeded database; all four indexes valid; rerun is a no-op.
95	- Depends on: none (test in T1.3). Estimate note: build time on a large table is unknown (FP-DB3).
96	
97	**T1.3 Test the migration** (agent, 1 to 1.5 h)
98	- Steps: `tests/integration/migration-0007.test.ts` per testing 0004 section 3.5 (no-transaction applies, indexes valid, interrupted-build leftover handled, inserts continue during build, drop rollback, build time recorded on 100k rows).
99	- Acceptance: test passes; recorded build time on the seed.
100	- Depends on: T1.1, T1.2.
101	
102	**T1.4 Change the compiler and write the operator-matrix tests** (agent, 3 to 4 h)
103	- Why: ADR-0031, 0033, 0035; search 0003 sections 4, 12; FP-2, FP-3, FP-8, FP-S5 to S8.
104	- Steps: in `src/lib/search/leaf.ts` and `compile.ts`: classify unquoted Latin terms of 3+ characters as `stem_sub`, under 3 as `short_stem` (stem only), quoted as `exact`, non-Latin unchanged. Emit for each side the exact index expressions (original side repeats the `split_part(...) IN ('en','und')` predicate; foreign originals use the substring and exact paths only), the translation side with `superseded_at IS NULL`, the summary side as an `EXISTS` over `derived_values` with `field = 'summary' AND is_current`. Use `plainto_tsquery('english', $n)` parameters. Stop-word-only terms fall back to substring or exact. NOT stays original-only (never stem OR summary). Return per-side predicates so `matched_in` can report a set.
105	- Where: `src/lib/search/leaf.ts`, `compile.ts`, `parse.ts` (no grammar change), tests in `tests/unit/search-compile-translation.test.ts` and `tests/unit/parse.test.ts`.
106	- Acceptance: operator-by-side matrix in testing 0004 section 3.2 passes; no string-built tsquery; expression text snapshot equals the migration text.
107	- Depends on: none. Human gate: read the generated SQL for one multi-term query.
108	
109	**T1.5 Update the list query and match sides** (agent, 2 to 3 h)
110	- Steps: in `src/lib/search/run.ts` add `left(tr.body_en, 600) AS body_excerpt_en`; replace the single `matched_in` with a set of sides (`original`, `translation`, `summary`) computed only for returned rows; keep keyset ordering. Expose `trgm_index` state to the search page response. Update the Search 0003 section 6 wording (C2).
111	- Where: `src/lib/search/run.ts`, `src/app/api/search/route.ts`, types used by `src/components/search/SearchPage.tsx`.
112	- Acceptance: response contains `body_excerpt_en` and `matched_in` sides; EXPLAIN shows the `CASE` is not evaluated for non-returned rows (E7 timing check).
113	- Depends on: T1.2, T1.4. Also verify in `src/worker/finish.ts` that a new summary flips the previous `is_current` (FP-DB6); fix only if wrong.
114	
115	**T1.6 Golden, plan and experiment tests** (agent with a human reading the plans, 3 to 4 h)
116	- Steps: `tests/integration/search-default-match.test.ts` (G1 to G17), `tests/integration/search-plans.test.ts` (P1 to P7, node-type assertions on a 20k seed), experiments E2 to E5, E9 to E11 recorded in `reports/` with environment details; run the first sizing experiment (index sizes and build times) and replace the guesses in DBA 0004 section 3; check 20 real summaries for language (Q1).
117	- Acceptance: all cases pass; recall 100 percent on G1, G3, G8; extra-hit report produced.
118	- Human checkpoint: a person reads the plans for stem OR substring, NOT, rare and common terms and chooses OR/EXISTS versus the UNION shape (HP-1, HP-S1, HP-DB2).
119	- Depends on: T1.3, T1.5.
120	
121	**T1.7 Benchmark B1 and review gate** (agent runs; human decides, 1 to 1.5 h)
122	- Steps: extend `.benchmarks/article-ingest/` (carma-benchmark) to compare insert rows/s with and without the four indexes at 100k rows; run carma-review on the diff.
123	- Acceptance: within 15 percent (proposed) or the cost is reported and accepted by the user (Q5).
124	- Depends on: T1.6.
125	Phase 1 exit: migration, compiler, query and tests pass; B1 recorded; review report written.
126	
127	### Phase 2: Display, echo, telemetry (about 10 to 15 hours)
128	Goal: English-first cards and article page, honest echo and match markers, signals and tests.
129	Entry criteria: Phase 1 exit; Q1 answered or defaulted.
130	Rollback or safe-stop: UI changes are independent per component; reverting the card or page returns the old layout without affecting search.
131	Human checkpoints: T2.2 look at cards with Arabic and Chinese data; T2.8 review.
132	
133	**T2.1 Write the headline-pair function** (agent, 1 to 1.5 h)
134	- Why: ADR-0032; FP-6, FP-7. Steps: pure function returning primary, secondary, language codes and note for every UX 0004 section 5.2 state, reusing the job-state mapping in `src/lib/translate/display.ts`. Tests: `tests/unit/headline-pair.test.ts`, extend `tests/unit/translate-display.test.ts`.
135	- Acceptance: all state rows covered; never an empty primary. Depends on: none.
136	
137	**T2.2 Rebuild the search card** (agent, 2 to 3 h)
138	- Steps: `src/components/ArticleCard.tsx`: English `h2` with `lang="en"`, original line labelled "Original (Arabic):", "Machine translated" tag (Q3), state notes, "Show more" → English excerpt, "Show original text" → original excerpt underneath, no-JS handling, summary `lang` fix (C7). Retire `englishHeadline` and related strings in `src/lib/ui/strings.ts`.
139	- Acceptance: component tests (testing 0004 section 3.3) pass; manual look at Arabic and Chinese cards at phone and desktop widths.
140	- Depends on: T1.5, T2.1.
141	
142	**T2.3 Rebuild the article-page text block** (agent, 2 h)
143	- Steps: `src/components/TranslatedText.tsx` and `src/app/articles/[id]/page.tsx`: headline pair, English body, native `<details>` revealing the original underneath (translation stays visible), remove swap and min-height trick, live announcement, beacon on `toggle`.
144	- Acceptance: stacked content, keyboard operable, works with JavaScript disabled. Depends on: T2.1.
145	
146	**T2.4 Echo, notes, strings, coverage line** (agent, 1.5 to 2 h)
147	- Steps: `src/lib/search/echo.ts` and `SearchPage.tsx`: quoted terms in quotes, loose-match note only with an unquoted Latin term, quote tip, changed NOT note, degraded-mode note, no-summary coverage line (Q2). Strings in `src/lib/ui/strings.ts`.
148	- Acceptance: echo tests (testing 0004 section 3.4); XSS check on terms. Depends on: T1.4.
149	
150	**T2.5 Update the matched-side marker** (agent, 1 h)
151	- Steps: `src/components/MatchedInTag.tsx` for sets of sides and summary copy (UX 0004 section 5.5). Acceptance: marker text per combination. Depends on: T1.5.
152	
153	**T2.6 Add beacon values, metrics, alerts, dashboards** (agent, 2 to 3 h)
154	- Steps: update the route `src/app/api/telemetry/translation-view/route.ts` (new values, keep legacy one release, Q6); add series in `src/lib/metrics.ts` (check `tests/unit/metrics-labels.test.ts`); emit from compiler, search route and status refresher; alerts E1 to E3 in `ops/alerts.yml`; Grafana search row in `ops/grafana/`; log fields without query text.
155	- Acceptance: beacon enum test (`tests/unit/translation-view-route.test.ts`); series visible on `/api/metrics`; alert rules load. Depends on: T1.5, T2.3.
156	
157	**T2.7 End-to-end tests** (agent, 1 to 1.5 h)
158	- Steps: Playwright: keyboard toggles, focus stays, no-JS article page reveal, card two-level reveal, RTL fixture. Where: `tests/e2e/smoke.spec.ts` or a new spec. Depends on: T2.2, T2.3.
159	
160	**T2.8 Benchmark B2, review gate, close-out** (agent plus human, 1.5 to 2 h)
161	- Steps: carma-benchmark for search latency by term kind (B2); carma-review on the phase diff; update README search syntax section; ask the user to approve the architect spec 0004 (then set approved and fix C1, C3).
162	- Acceptance: B2 within thresholds in testing 0004 section 5; review report in `.specs/review/`.
163	- Depends on: T2.2 to T2.7.
164	Phase 2 exit: all tests in testing 0004 section 11 pass.
